newsitem.title: UK: EU feud, poll depress Britain's Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: EU feud, poll depress Britain's Conservatives.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major faced a battle to restore the unity of his Conservative Party on Tuesday as his members of parliament bickered over Europe and an opinion poll cast gloom over his supporters.

The poll, in the Guardian newspaper, suggested that last week's budget containing a penny in the pound off the standard rate of income tax, had harmed the ruling party rather than giving it the electoral boost it desperately needed.

With less than six months to go before Major must call a general election, the poll by the ICM group showed the gap between the Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party had widened by six points in the past month to Labour 19 points ahead.

"We have to be cautious about drawing conclusions from a single poll," said one elections expert. "But if this trend is confirmed (by other polls), it is hard to see how the Tories (Conservatives) can hope to stay in power."
Finance minister Kenneth Clarke, the man who framed the budget and the cabinet's leading pro-European, was at the centre of the latest round of infighting over Europe within the party.
On Monday, Clarke reacted furiously to a newspaper story saying Major might rule out Britain joining a single European currency within the next five years ahead of the general election due by May.
Such a move, he told an interviewer, would be "senseless", recalling that October's Conservative Party conference had accepted Major's wait-and-see stance on the single currency.

Newspapers differed on Tuesday on the significance of Clarke's statement. "Major lets Clarke fume," was the verdict of the Daily Mail which said the chancellor of the exchequer (Clarke) was isolated in the cabinet on the issue.
But the Independent, arguing that Major could not afford the resignation of his finance minister in the run-up to an election, saw Clarke as now having a "Euro armlock on Major".

John Redwood, the Eurosceptic former cabinet minister who last year challenged Major for the party leadership, told the BBC if the prime minister chose to rule out jettisoning the pound, a clear majority of his cabinet would back him.
"The question is whether he judges that right now and whether he wishes to take that to cabinet," Redwood said.
Pro-European Conservative MP Quentin Davies made it clear Major would encounter fierce opposition from his side of the party if he came off the fence against a single currency.

"It would be completely crazy and contrary to the national interest to throw away our option to join the single currency. The British people would not respect a government that did such an irresponsible thing," he said.
Labour, trying to play down its reputation as a tax-and-spend party, plan to abstain in the parliamentary vote on Clarke's budget scheduled for 2200 GMT on Tuesday.
But the party is looking forward to a December 12 by-election in the rock-solid Labour seat of Barnsley East which is certain to end Major's overall parliamentary majority.
That, Labour believes, will give it a chance to harry the Conservatives in parliament and maybe force an early election.
